summary: Specifies how to carry IPv6, IPv4, and ARP packets over Fibre Channel. It also describes how to form IPv6 link-local and autoconfigured addresses on Fibre Channel and how to resolve IPv4 addresses there. It obsoletes RFC 2625 and RFC 3831, and was later updated by RFC 5494 and RFC 8064.

eli5.summary: Fibre Channel is a fast road built for storage gear. This explains how to load ordinary internet traffic onto it and how devices there get their addresses.

questions: how does ip work over fibre channel
what is the default mtu for ip over fibre channel
subtitle: How IPv6, IPv4 and ARP packets ride inside Fibre Channel frames, and how devices there find each other.

tldr.problem: Fibre Channel is a storage network, not an IP network. RFC 2625 covered IPv4 and ARP over it for only a subset of devices, and RFC 3831 covered IPv6 separately.
tldr.mechanism: Each IP or ARP packet is wrapped in a 16-octet Network_Header and an 8-octet LLC/SNAP header, then sent as a Fibre Channel Sequence in Class 3 frames. IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery and IPv4 uses a Fibre Channel specific ARP that carries both the N_Port_Name and the N_Port_ID.
tldr.outcome: One document now covers IPv6, IPv4 and ARP for all the N_Port_Name formats in use. It obsoletes RFC 2625 and RFC 3831 and was later updated by RFC 5494 and RFC 8064.

today: RFC 4338 is a Proposed Standard. It obsoleted RFC 2625 and RFC 3831, and it has since been updated by RFC 5494 and RFC 8064.

sections.title: Why One Document Replaces Two
sections.content:
Fibre Channel (FC) is a high-speed serial interface technology that supports several upper layer protocols, including SCSI, IPv6 and IPv4. RFC 2625 had defined IPv4 and ARP over Fibre Channel for a subset of devices, and RFC 3831 had defined IPv6. This RFC merges the two and obsoletes both.

The RFC names three limits of RFC 2625 that it resolves. IPv4 was restricted to devices with a format 0x1 N_Port_Name, although many implementations used other formats. FARP, the Fibre Channel Address Resolution Protocol, was required to map names to addresses, although many implementations used other methods such as the Fibre Channel Name Server. And IPv4 multicast was not specified at all.

The RFC also warns readers who know Fibre Channel that both FC and IETF standards use the same byte transmission order, but the bit numbering differs. Appendix C gives guidance.
sections.eli5: There used to be two rulebooks for putting internet traffic on this storage road, one for the old internet and one for the new one. This RFC replaces both with a single, simpler rulebook.

sections.title: Fibre Channel in Brief
sections.content:
Fibre Channel is a gigabit-speed network technology used mainly for storage networking. A Node has one or more Ports. A port that does not run in a loop is an N_Port, one in a loop is an NL_Port, and Nx_Port covers both. Ports can be joined by a point-to-point link, a switched Fabric, or a loop. The RFC treats the whole network as a multiaccess network with broadcast: to IPv6 it is a Link, and to IPv4 it is a Local Network.

Every Nx_Port has two identifiers. The N_Port_Name is a non-volatile 64-bit name. The N_Port_ID is a volatile 24-bit address that is used to send frames. A port gets its N_Port_ID by Fabric Login (FLOGI), and two ports must complete a Port Login (PLOGI) before they communicate effectively. The first four bits of a name give its format.

An IP packet is an Information Unit at the FC-4 level. The FC-2 level maps it to a Sequence of one or more frames, and the frame data field can be 0 to 2112 octets. Sequences that belong together are grouped into an Exchange, identified by an originator ID (OX_ID) and a responder ID (RX_ID).
sections.eli5: Every device on this network has a permanent name, like your real name, and a temporary number, like a seat number that can change. Big messages are cut into pieces called frames and put back together on the other side.

sections.title: Encapsulation of IP and ARP Packets
sections.content:
An Information Unit carrying an IPv6, IPv4 or ARP packet MUST carry the FC Network_Header (16 octets: destination and source N_Port_Name) and an LLC/SNAP header (8 octets). Only the first frame of a multi-frame Sequence carries these two headers. Later frames carry just more of the packet. An ARP packet is small enough to fit in a single frame.

The FC ESP_Header MAY be used to secure the frames. No other optional headers may be used. The FC header uses fixed code points: R_CTL 0x04, TYPE 0x05 (IP over Fibre Channel), and DF_CTL 0x20 for the first frame (0x00 for later frames), or 0x60 and 0x40 when ESP is used.

The LLC/SNAP header uses DSAP 0xAA, SSAP 0xAA, CTRL 0x03 and OUI 0x000000. The PID is 0x86DD for IPv6, 0x0800 for IPv4 and 0x0806 for ARP. Class 3 (datagram service) is required for multicast and control traffic and recommended for other unicast IP traffic.

The default MTU is 65280 octets for both IPv6 and IPv4, and it can be reduced by manual configuration, by Router Advertisements (IPv6) or by Path MTU Discovery. IPv6 must never go below 1280 octets, so an Nx_Port MUST handle an Information Unit of at least 1304 octets (1280 + 8 + 16).
sections.eli5: Each internet packet goes into an envelope with two labels: one with the sender and receiver names, and one saying what kind of letter is inside. Only the first piece of a long message needs the labels.

sections.title: IPv6 Addresses from N_Port_Names
sections.content:
The IPv6 Interface Identifier of an Nx_Port comes from the EUI-64 address derived from its N_Port_Name, with the Universal/Local bit of the OUI complemented. This works for N_Port_Name formats 0x1, 0x2 and 0x5, which map to EUI-64 directly, and for the EUI-64 mapped formats 0xC to 0xF, which can be reversed. Stateless address autoconfiguration follows the standard procedure and the prefix MUST be 64 bits long.

The RFC walks through each case. For example, the format 0x1 name 0x10-00-34-63-46-AB-CD-EF gives the interface identifier 3463:461A:BCDE:F000. Identifiers from formats 0x1, 0x2 and 0x5 have local scope, while those from EUI-64 mapped names have global scope.

The link-local address is the interface identifier appended to the prefix FE80::/64.
sections.eli5: Your device already has a permanent name. The rules say how to turn that name into an internet address by shuffling a few bits, so nobody has to hand out addresses.

sections.title: Finding Link-layer Addresses
sections.content:
Resolving an address means finding both the N_Port_Name and the N_Port_ID, since both are needed. The link-layer address (also called the hardware address in ARP) is 12 octets: the 8-octet N_Port_Name, a reserved octet that is zero on send and ignored on receipt, and the 3-octet N_Port_ID.

For IPv6, Neighbor Discovery is used. The Source/Target Link-layer Address option has Type 1 (source) or 2 (target), Length 2 (units of 8 octets), the link-layer address, and zero padding.

For IPv4, the RFC defines an FC ARP format, 40 octets long, with HW Type 0x0012 (IANA registered hardware type 18), Protocol 0x0800, HW Len 12 and Proto Len 4. The source port first checks its local mapping table. If there is no mapping, or no valid Port Login, it broadcasts an FC ARP Request. The port with the matching IPv4 address caches the sender, and, logging in first if needed, sends a unicast reply. If no port matches, no reply is sent.
sections.eli5: To mail a letter you need a person's name and their current seat number. A broadcast question asks everyone, who has this internet address, and the right device answers with both.

sections.title: Multicast, Sequences and Exchanges
sections.content:
IPv6 multicast, IPv4 multicast and broadcast, and ARP broadcast packets MUST be sent to the broadcast N_Port_ID 0xFFFFFF in Class 3. The destination N_Port_Name in the Network_Header says what kind of group it is: 0x10-00-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF for ARP and IPv4 broadcast, 0x10-00-33-33-XX-YY-ZZ-QQ for IPv6 multicast, and 0x10-00-01-00-5E-XX-YY-ZZ for IPv4 multicast. The receive data field size of the implicit Port Login for broadcast SHOULD be 1024 octets, and must be the same across the Fabric.

Sequences MUST be non-streamed, and SEQ_CNT MUST increase continuously, starting at zero in the first frame of an Exchange. Packets are sent in dedicated unidirectional Exchanges: the Sequence Initiative bit is zero and RX_ID is 0xFFFF. Unicast control packets (ARP, ICMP, Neighbor Discovery, IGMP and the like) SHOULD use short-lived Exchanges with one Sequence. Unicast data traffic MUST use a long-lived Exchange.

Appendix A explains how to send a broadcast Sequence over each topology. Appendix B explains why a port MUST re-validate the name-to-ID mapping after events like a loop initialization or a link outage, because the N_Port_ID is volatile.
sections.eli5: To shout to everyone at once, you send to a special address that means everybody. Messages between two devices go on their own private lane, one way only, and each piece is numbered so the order stays right.

sections.title: Compatibility with RFC 2625
sections.content:
The IPv4 encapsulation, Exchange handling and Sequence handling are the same as in RFC 2625, so implementations are expected to interoperate for sending and receiving IPv4 packets. The main difference is address resolution: RFC 2625 uses the Ethernet ARP format and requires format 0x1 N_Port_Names, and this RFC does not use FARP.

A port with another name format can talk to an RFC 2625 device by manual configuration of the mapping, though not if that device strictly insists on format 0x1. A port with a format 0x1 name can also use compatibility mode: it MUST send two ARP Requests, first in FC ARP format and then in Ethernet ARP format, and MUST answer an Ethernet ARP Request with an Ethernet ARP Reply. It MAY answer FARP requests. Compatibility mode is REQUIRED to be supported and MUST be administratively configurable.
sections.eli5: Older devices speak an older dialect. The new rules let a device ask in both dialects, if an administrator turns that on, so everyone still understands each other.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The RFC says IPv6, IPv4 and ARP introduce no security concerns beyond those already present in Fibre Channel. It notes one practical consequence: soft zoning based on FC Name Server masking does not work with IPv4 and IPv6, because they do not use the Name Server.

The FC ESP_Header may be used to secure frames, and all the usual IP-layer security techniques may be used. For IANA, the ARP parameters directory was updated to reference this document for hardware type 18.
sections.eli5: Putting internet traffic on this network does not add new dangers. One storage-network safety trick does not work for it, but the usual internet locks can be used.
